extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), USPTO examiners, and inventors drafting AI-related patent applications (U.S.)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and assessing U.S. patent claims for AI-related inventions focused on whether claims are directed to an abstract idea or to a patent-eligible technological improvement, illustrated by USPTO Examples 47–49.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform abstract idea into a practical technological application
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guidance assumes many AI-based method claims are abstract ideas; the central inquiry is whether the claim transforms that abstract idea into a practical technological application (i.e., a patent-eligible technological improvement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus examination on whether claimed elements integrate the abstract idea into a specific, practical technological solution rather than merely reciting the abstract idea itself. Examples 47–49 illustrate claims that fail or succeed on this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that generically recite training/using AI models are likely abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that generally refer to training an AI model and using the model to detect patterns or analyze data are less likely to survive subject-matter eligibility review because they are treated as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid high-level recitations like 'train a model' and 'use the model to detect patterns' without further technical integration or specific applications; include additional claim elements showing how the model is applied to a concrete technological problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciting specific, practical uses of AI analysis results supports eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that explicitly recite practical uses of the results of AI analysis—i.e., how detected information is used to effect a technological outcome—are more likely to be found eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 47 Claim 3 was found eligible because it required using detected anomaly information to detect source addresses, drop potentially malicious packets, and block future traffic—concrete actions that convert abstract detection into a technological response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specially customized physical structure (hardware) can render claim eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that require a specially customized physical structure (e.g., an ASIC with particular neuron/register/microprocessor organization) are more likely to be eligible because they recite a non-abstract physical device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 47 Claim 1 (an ANN implemented as an ASIC with specified components) was found eligible under this principle; drafting that includes physical/hardware limitations or specially configured circuitry can strengthen eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method claims must disclose how steps are performed (sufficient detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: High-level method steps (e.g., 'train ANN', 'detect anomalies', 'analyze anomalies') without details on how those steps are performed may be found ineligible for lacking inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 47 Claim 2 was found ineligible for failing to describe how training, detecting, and analyzing steps are performed. Provide technical detail about algorithms, data flows, or processing that demonstrate how the steps effect a technological improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using detected information to effect concrete actions adds an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that use detected or classified information to trigger specific corrective or control actions (e.g., dropping packets, blocking addresses) add an inventive concept beyond mere abstract classification/detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to show downstream application of the AI output in specific operational steps that change system behavior or accomplish a technical control function; Example 47 Claim 3 illustrates this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must reflect a technical improvement, not merely a mathematical operation
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that performs mathematical operations or data transformations (e.g., feature determination) but does not sufficiently integrate those operations into a technical improvement is likely abstract and ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 48 Claim 1 (speech separation DNN determining features) was ineligible because it was treated as a mathematical operation not integrated into a technical improvement; ensure claims tie algorithmic steps to improvements in system performance, signal processing, or other technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciting particular processing steps or outputs that give a concrete improvement supports eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite particular processing steps (e.g., synthesizing speech waveforms from masked clusters, combining waveforms to generate a mixed signal, transmitting for remote storage) can show a 'particular' improvement over prior methods and be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 48 Claim 2 was eligible because the claimed steps (synthesizing and combining waveforms, remote storage) were specific technical operations tied to an improvement. Include specific processing actions and concrete outputs in claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering of steps and specifying how training aids downstream processing can add inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that detail the ordering of steps and how a trained model specifically aids subsequent assignments or processing can direct the claim to a technical improvement despite some abstract elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 48 Claim 3 was eligible because it recited details of how DNN training aids cluster assignments and the ordering of steps; draft claims to show interdependence and particular roles of processing stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vague treatment steps that do not meaningfully limit claims are ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad or vague steps like administering 'an appropriate treatment' that do not require any particular application of the abstract idea generally fail eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 49 Claim 1 was ineligible because step (c) 'administering an appropriate treatment' did not meaningfully limit the claim. Replace vague, catch‑all functional language with specific treatments or concrete therapeutic actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciting a specific, particular treatment can convert an abstract idea into a patent-eligible application
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a short, specific limitation identifying a particular treatment (e.g., 'wherein the appropriate treatment is Compound X eye drops') can transform a claim from abstract to a particular, patent-eligible medical treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 49 Claim 2 became eligible by naming a specific treatment; consider claiming particular compounds, dosages, or concrete medical interventions when appropriate to ground a claim in a concrete application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing only faster classification or shorter time may be insufficient without demonstrating improvement to a computer or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure that an AI model determines a risk score or provides classification 'in less time' does not necessarily show an improvement to the functioning of a computer or other technology and may be insufficient for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how performance improvements translate to technological improvements (e.g., reduced resource usage, improved signal fidelity, reduced latency that enables a new technical effect) rather than merely faster results in the abstract; the sufficiency of such disclosure remains subject to interpretation.
